builder_plan.scenario: A workflow needs specialist review, but extra agents may add more cost than useful work.
builder_plan.change: Test the proposed division of work against a single-agent implementation.
builder_plan.baseline: One agent with the same tools and an equal total token and time budget.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Accepted outputs, coordination failures, wall-clock time, and total cost across all agents.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Iterated creation, grading, and revision of data science projects by language models
summary: The technique replaces single-pass agent execution with a loop in which a writer LLM produces a data science project, a grader LLM scores it, and the writer revises across three rounds. It costs roughly three times the API tokens, latency, and tool-call budget of a single pass, plus the engineering to execute submissions and manage grading, with no local GPU requirement. It can fail because much of the measured improvement is grader noise, self-grading is biased upward, gains are highly model- and pairing-dependent, and weaker graders do not improve stronger writers.
rationale: The loop is cheap to implement on API-only infrastructure and shows real average gains, but the large variance across model pairings and grader noise means the reader must validate the specific writer-grader combination on their own workload before relying on it.
technique: Iterative writer-grader revision loop for data science agents

claims.statement: The technique replaces single-pass agent execution with a loop in which a writer LLM produces a data science project, a grader LLM scores it, and the writer revises across three rounds. It costs roughly three times the API tokens, latency, and tool-call budget of a single pass, plus the engineering to execute submissions and manage grading, with no local GPU requirement. It can fail because much of the measured improvement is grader noise, self-grading is biased upward, gains are highly model- and pairing-dependent, and weaker graders do not improve stronger writers.

Average score rises from 59% to 76% over three feedback rounds; gains vary by model from 3 to 46 percentage points, with self-grading inflating scores by about 9 points and roughly half of round-to-round differences attributable to grader noise.
